text:
Africa needs more electricity infrastructure. It also needs to see and operate the infrastructure it already has.

Our latest research looks at digital grid modernisation: meters, asset records, telemetry, remote control, grid-enhancing technologies and AI.

The starting point matters. Sub-Saharan African transmission and distribution losses were equivalent to 26% of electricity output in 2024. Nigeria's customer metering rate was 61.51% in June 2026. At the same time, 590 million people across Africa still lack electricity access.

That combination creates a temptation to jump straight to the newest technology. We think the better question is simpler: what is the lowest missing layer stopping the network from working better?

StoneComms proposes a five-level Digital Grid Readiness Ladder: truth, observation, action, market and intelligence.

First, utilities need a trusted model of the network: assets, customers, feeders and transformers that match physical reality. Then they need meters and sensors to observe it. Then remote controls and operating systems to act on what they see. Only after those foundations are reliable do flexibility markets, digital twins and AI become genuinely useful.

This is not an argument against advanced technology. The IEA estimates that dynamic ratings, topology optimisation and advanced power-flow control could release very large amounts of capacity globally. But software cannot compensate for an unmapped feeder, an unmetered customer or a utility that cannot recover its costs.

For investors, funders and utilities, the practical implication is to sequence digital spending around operational constraints rather than technology fashion.
